extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent practitioners and applicants (especially for business-method and computer-implemented inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent claims under the USPTO 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (IEG) and follow-on guidance, with business-method examples showing how to apply Steps 1, 2A, and 2B (including case-law comparisons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'The system comprises a device or set of devices and, therefore, is a machine, which is a statutory category of invention (Step 1: YES).' If the claim recites a statutory category, proceed to analyze whether it is directed to a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception such as a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'The claim is then analyzed to determine if the claim is directed to a judicial exception.' Use case-law analogies (e.g., organizing human behavior, collecting/recognizing/storing data, mathematical correlations) to identify abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: No exception recited -> eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim does not recite any judicial exception, that alone may be sufficient for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As noted: 'It is important to point out as well that there is no apparent exception recited in the claim, which alone would be sufficient for eligibility.' Examiners may note this in an Office action or reasons for allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim 'directed to' vs merely 'involving' an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish whether a claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea (ending eligibility analysis) or only 'involves' it (may still be eligible under Step 2A if claim is an improvement in computer-related technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Enfish and BASCOM discussions — if a claim is 'directed to' a non-abstract improvement (e.g., an improvement in computer functionality), the Step 2A inquiry may end with eligibility. The Federal Circuit described some claims as a 'close call' and examiners should consider whether the claim is clearly an Internet-centric problem or a computer-technology improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are analyzed under their broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification (especially during examination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'All of the claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation.' Apply plain meaning absent special definitions in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any element or combination of elements ensures the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the exception (the inventive concept inquiry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'Under Step 2B, the claim as a whole is analyzed to determine whether any element, or combination of elements, is sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.' Consider both individual elements and the ordered combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer/Internet components insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely recite generic computer, network, and Internet components performing conventional functions do not amount to 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'These limitations do not amount to significantly more when taken individually, [because they] recite generic computer, network and Internet components, none of which is inventive by itself.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconventional/non-generic combination can supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: An unconventional and non-generic combination of known elements can supply the inventive concept that makes the claim 'significantly more' than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'Here, an inventive concept can be found in the unconventional and non-generic combination of known elements, and more specifically “the installation of a filtering tool at a specific location, remote from the end-users, with customizable filtering features specific to each end-user”.' Evaluate whether the ordered combination yields an improvement in technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered-combination analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze additional claim limitations not only individually but as an ordered combination to determine whether they amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'The analysis under Step 2B (also called the “inventive concept inquiry”) requires more than determining that each additional claim element ... is well known by itself.' The claim must be considered 'when viewed as an ordered combination.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-based solution / improvement to technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that provide a technology-based solution that improves the functioning of a computer or other technology — and that overcome prior-art problems — are more likely to be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'The claimed arrangement of elements in the system results in an improvement in the technology of filtering content on the Internet' and 'a “technology-based solution” of filtering content on the Internet that overcomes the problems in the prior art'. Use specification and factual record to show how the claimed arrangement solves technical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare to relevant case law to identify abstract idea vs improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use comparisons to Federal Circuit and Supreme Court decisions (e.g., Enfish, BASCOM, DDR, OIP, Content Extraction, Intellectual Ventures I, Ultramercial, Accenture) to determine whether the claim is abstract or a technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance provides detailed case-law contrasts (e.g., claims that are 'simply the generic automation of traditional techniques' are not technology-based solutions). A case-law comparison can be informative but is not mandatory during examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping claim focus to known abstract-idea categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the focus of the claim maps to abstract-idea categories (e.g., methods of organizing human behavior, collecting/recognizing/storing data, mathematical correlations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'Filtering content is ... a “method of organizing human behavior” that is similar to other concepts that have been identified as abstract by the courts.' Use analogies to prior abstract-idea holdings to support Step 2A conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific meaningful limitations implementing the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional claim elements that are specific, meaningful, and implement the abstract idea in a particular way can supply the inventive concept and render the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from ATM hypotheticals: claims that 'generate a random code and transmit it to a mobile communication device ... read an image ... decrypt code data ... and control access to the keypad' were found to have specific meaningful limitations and thus were eligible (Claims 2 and 3), whereas a generic recitation of steps (Claim 1) was ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: If the record warrants, add explanatory remarks in Office action or reasons for allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may add remarks to an Office action or reasons for allowance to clarify why a claim is not directed to a judicial exception or why it is eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: 'If the examiner believes that the record would benefit from clarification, remarks could be added to an Office action or reasons for allowance, indicating that the claim is not directed to any judicial exception.' This is a procedural suggestion for examiners to document positions.
